On a warm afternoon the aeroplane at a 5,000 ft airport takes off as if the runway were at 8,250 ft: a longer ground roll, a slower climb and less power from a normally aspirated engine.

The 120 ft rule is linear, and the real relationship is not. Computed from the ICAO Standard Atmosphere, the density altitude for this case is about 8,050 ft, some 200 ft lower than the rule of thumb. Here the rule errs on the cautious side, and the size of the gap changes with altitude and temperature, which is one reason to use a computed value for performance planning. Humidity raises density altitude a little and is in neither figure.

#### How do you solve the wind triangle?

You know your true course, your true airspeed, and the wind. You want the heading to hold and the groundspeed you will make.

Worked example: true course 090°, true airspeed 120 kt, wind from 160° at 30 kt.

1. **Wind angle** between the course and the wind direction: 160 − 90 = 70°, from the right.
2. **Wind correction angle:** sin(WCA) = 30 × sin 70° ÷ 120 = 0.235, so WCA = **13.6°**. The wind is from the right, so correct to the right.
3. **True heading:** 090 + 13.6 = **104°**.
4. **Groundspeed:** 120 × cos 13.6° − 30 × cos 70° = 116.6 − 10.3 = **106 kt**.

The formulas:

- **WCA = arcsin( wind speed × sin(wind angle) ÷ TAS )**
- **Groundspeed = TAS × cos(WCA) − wind speed × cos(wind angle)**

Then apply magnetic variation and compass deviation to turn the true heading into the one you fly.

#### How do you find the crosswind component for landing?

Same trigonometry, with the runway in place of the course.

**Crosswind = wind speed × sin(angle between wind and runway)**
**Headwind = wind speed × cos(angle)**

| Angle off the runway | Crosswind as a share of wind speed |
|---|---|
| 10° | 17% |
| 20° | 34% |
| 30° | 50% |
| 45° | 71% |
| 60° | 87% |
| 90° | 100% |

Runway 27 with the wind 300° at 20 kt: the angle is 30°, so the crosswind is **10 kt** and the headwind 17 kt. Compare the crosswind with the maximum demonstrated crosswind in your aircraft's handbook, and with your own limits. Runway numbers are magnetic, and tower and ATIS winds are magnetic; winds in METARs and forecasts are true.

#### Why does true airspeed differ from indicated airspeed?

The airspeed indicator measures the pressure of the air hitting the pitot tube, and thin air pushes less. At altitude the aeroplane is moving faster through the air than the needle shows. A common approximation is that true airspeed is about 2% higher than calibrated airspeed for each 1,000 ft of density altitude. At a density altitude of 8,000 ft, 110 kt calibrated is about 124 kt true; the rule of thumb gives 128. The exact figure comes from the air density at your pressure altitude and temperature.

#### Where does TrueCourse E6B fit?

[TrueCourse E6B](https://aisixteen.com/truecourse-e6b/) is an E6B flight computer for student pilots, GA pilots and CFIs. It solves the wind triangle with a live vector diagram (heading, groundspeed, wind correction angle and the crosswind and headwind components), true airspeed and Mach, density, pressure and true altitude, a nav log, fuel, climb and descent, and weight and balance with a CG envelope. Its numbers come from published formulas in the FAA-H-8083 handbooks and the ICAO Standard Atmosphere. It works offline with no account. It is a training and planning aid: the aircraft's flight manual and current official weather remain the authority for any flight.

#### Frequently asked questions

##### What is the formula for density altitude?

A common approximation is pressure altitude + 120 × (outside air temperature − standard temperature), in feet and °C. Standard temperature is 15 °C minus 2 °C per 1,000 ft of pressure altitude.

##### How do you calculate crosswind quickly?

Multiply the wind speed by the sine of the angle between the wind and the runway: half the wind at 30°, about 70% at 45°, nearly all of it at 60° and beyond.

##### Does humidity affect density altitude?

Yes, slightly. Humid air is less dense than dry air at the same pressure and temperature, so it raises density altitude. The standard formulas ignore it.

#### Sources

- FAA, *Pilot's Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge* (FAA-H-8083-25), chapters on flight instruments, aircraft performance and navigation: [faa.gov](https://www.faa.gov/regulations_policies/handbooks_manuals/aviation/phak)
- ICAO Doc 7488, *Manual of the ICAO Standard Atmosphere*.

### How can you tell whether the aurora will be visible tonight?

URL: https://aisixteen.com/earth-around/blog/will-the-aurora-be-visible-tonight/ · App: Earth Around (https://aisixteen.com/earth-around/) · Published: 2026-11-24

Short answer: Check three things in order: the forecast Kp and view line for tonight, then, on the night, whether the solar wind's Bz is pointing south and staying there, then your own sky: darkness, cloud and a clear view toward the pole. Solar wind readings give roughly 30 to 60 minutes of warning.

An aurora forecast is really several forecasts with different ranges. Some look days ahead and are rough; one looks less than an hour ahead and is quite good. Knowing which is which tells you when to go to bed and when to put your boots on.

#### What actually causes an aurora?

Charged particles from the Sun flow past Earth as the solar wind, carrying a magnetic field with them. When that field points south, opposite to Earth's field on the day side, the two connect and energy is loaded into Earth's magnetic tail. When it is released, electrons run down the field lines and hit the upper atmosphere at about 100 to 300 km, where oxygen and nitrogen glow: green and red from oxygen, blue and purple from nitrogen.

The light forms a ring around each magnetic pole, the auroral oval. More energy makes the oval brighter and pushes it toward the equator. Every forecast is an estimate of where that oval will be.

#### How far ahead can each forecast see?

| What you check | Looks ahead | How reliable | What it tells you |
|---|---|---|---|
| Coronal hole or eruption seen on the Sun | 1 to 4 days | Rough: arrival times can be off by half a day, and the field direction is unknown | Whether a night is worth keeping free |
| Kp forecast and tonight's view line | Hours to 3 days | Moderate | How far from the pole the aurora might reach |
| Solar wind at L1: speed, density, Bz | About 30 to 60 minutes | Good | Whether it is about to start |
| The sky itself | Now | Certain | Whether you can see it |

#### Why is Bz the number to watch?

Bz is the north–south part of the magnetic field in the solar wind. It is the switch.

- **Bz south (negative):** the door is open. Around −5 nT sustained is enough for activity at high latitudes; −10 nT or lower, held for an hour or more, is storm material.
- **Bz north (positive):** the door is mostly closed, even if the wind is fast.

Speed and density set how much arrives while the door is open. A quiet wind is 300 to 500 km/s; above 600 km/s with southward Bz is a strong combination.

Bz can flip in minutes, which is why a promising evening can go quiet and a dull one can light up. Watch the trend over the last half hour, not a single reading.

#### How much warning do solar wind readings give?

The solar wind is measured by spacecraft at the L1 point, about 1.5 million km from Earth toward the Sun. The warning is the time the wind takes to cover that distance:

| Solar wind speed | Travel time from L1 |
|---|---|
| 400 km/s | about 62 minutes |
| 500 km/s | about 50 minutes |
| 600 km/s | about 42 minutes |
| 800 km/s | about 31 minutes |

So the faster and more promising the wind, the less warning you get. NOAA's short-term aurora model, OVATION, takes those L1 measurements and produces a map of the oval for roughly the next 30 to 90 minutes.

#### What is the view line?

The view line is the edge of where an aurora might be *seen*, which is farther from the pole than where it is overhead. Because the light is 100 km or more up, an aurora overhead at one place can be seen low on the horizon from several hundred kilometres toward the equator. NOAA publishes a view line for tonight and tomorrow night. If you are near the line, expect a glow or pillars low on the poleward horizon rather than curtains overhead.

#### Does a high Kp guarantee an aurora where I am?

No. Kp is a planet-wide, three-hour average. It tells you how far the oval reached, not what was above you at 23:10. You can miss a display at Kp 7 under cloud, and people at high latitudes see aurora most clear nights at Kp 2. Use Kp to answer "is it my latitude's turn?" and Bz to answer "is it happening now?".

#### What on the ground still decides it?

- **Darkness.** The sky has to be properly dark. At high latitudes in summer it never is, which is why the aurora season runs from late August to April.
- **Cloud.** Aurora is far above all weather. Solid cloud ends the night.
- **Light pollution and the Moon.** A faint aurora is easily lost in city glow or under a full Moon. Get a dark horizon toward the pole.
- **Time of night.** Activity is most likely in the hours around local midnight, though strong storms ignore the clock.
- **Time of year.** Geomagnetic activity is statistically higher in the weeks around the March and September equinoxes.
- **Your eyes.** Give them 15 to 20 minutes in the dark. A faint aurora looks grey-white to the eye; a phone camera on a long exposure will show the green first.

#### A simple routine for the night

1. **Afternoon:** look at the forecast Kp and tonight's view line. If the line is far poleward of you, relax.
2. **After dark:** check cloud, then check Bz and speed. Southward and steady, go out.
3. **Outside:** look toward the pole, low on the horizon, and wait. Displays come in bursts of 10 to 30 minutes with quiet gaps between.

#### Where does Earth Around fit?

[Earth Around](https://aisixteen.com/earth-around/) puts the inputs for this routine in one place: tonight's aurora chance with the view line, solar wind speed and Bz, Kp, and Hp30 at 30-minute resolution, from NOAA and GFZ feeds. It is on iPhone, iPad, Mac and Apple Watch, including watch complications. It needs a connection for live readings, and it has no account and no tracking. It does not know your cloud cover or how dark your sky is; that part is yours.

Background: [what Kp and the NOAA G, R and S scales mean](https://aisixteen.com/earth-around/blog/kp-index-and-noaa-g-scale/).

#### Frequently asked questions

##### What Bz is good for aurora?

Negative, meaning southward. Around −5 nT sustained helps at high latitudes; −10 nT or lower for an hour or more usually means a storm.

##### How long before an aurora do you get a warning?

About 30 to 60 minutes from solar wind measurements at L1, less when the wind is fast. Forecasts days ahead exist but are rough.

##### What Kp do I need to see the aurora?

It depends on your magnetic latitude. Near the Arctic Circle, Kp 1 to 3 is often enough; the northern United States and northern Europe typically need Kp 5 to 7; lower latitudes need a severe storm.

#### Sources

- NOAA Space Weather Prediction Center, Aurora 30-Minute Forecast (OVATION): [swpc.noaa.gov/products/aurora-30-minute-forecast](https://www.swpc.noaa.gov/products/aurora-30-minute-forecast)
- NOAA Space Weather Prediction Center, Aurora Viewline for Tonight and Tomorrow Night: [swpc.noaa.gov](https://www.swpc.noaa.gov/products/aurora-viewline-tonight-and-tomorrow-night-experimental)
- NOAA Space Weather Prediction Center, Real Time Solar Wind: [swpc.noaa.gov/products/real-time-solar-wind](https://www.swpc.noaa.gov/products/real-time-solar-wind)
- Russell and McPherron, "Semiannual variation of geomagnetic activity", *Journal of Geophysical Research*, 1973: [doi.org/10.1029/JA078i001p00092](https://doi.org/10.1029/JA078i001p00092)

### What do the Kp index and the NOAA G, R and S scales mean?

URL: https://aisixteen.com/earth-around/blog/kp-index-and-noaa-g-scale/ · App: Earth Around (https://aisixteen.com/earth-around/) · Published: 2026-11-24

Short answer: Kp is a 0 to 9 index of how disturbed the Earth's magnetic field is over three hours. NOAA's G scale names the storm level from it: Kp 5 is G1 (minor), 6 is G2, 7 is G3, 8 is G4 and 9 is G5 (extreme). R rates radio blackouts from flares; S rates radiation storms.

Space weather reports use a handful of numbers that look alike and measure different things. This guide separates them: what each one measures, where it comes from, and what a given level means in practice.

![Earth Around dashboard with the NOAA space weather scales, planetary Kp chart and solar wind readings](https://aisixteen.com/eartharound/screenshot-960.webp "Earth Around: the NOAA scales first, then the numbers behind them.")

#### What is the Kp index?

Kp is the planetary K index. Thirteen magnetic observatories around the world each measure how far the horizontal magnetic field strayed from its quiet-day curve during a three-hour window. Each station turns that range into a local K value, and the values are combined into one planetary number from 0 (quiet) to 9 (extreme).

Three things follow from how it is built:

- **It is quasi-logarithmic.** Each step up means a much larger disturbance, not an equal one.
- **It covers three hours.** A short, violent disturbance and a long, moderate one can give the same Kp.
- **The official value comes later.** The definitive Kp is produced by GFZ, the German Research Centre for Geosciences in Potsdam. NOAA publishes its own estimated Kp in near real time, which is what most live displays show.

#### How does Kp map to the NOAA G scale?

The G scale is NOAA's public storm scale for geomagnetic storms. It is a direct relabelling of Kp from 5 upward.

| G level | Name | Kp | Average frequency per 11-year cycle | Aurora may be seen as low as (NOAA's examples) |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| G1 | Minor | 5 | 1,700 storms (900 days) | Northern Michigan and Maine |
| G2 | Moderate | 6 | 600 (360 days) | New York and Idaho |
| G3 | Strong | 7 | 200 (130 days) | Illinois and Oregon |
| G4 | Severe | 8, including 9− | 100 (60 days) | Alabama and northern California |
| G5 | Extreme | 9 | 4 (4 days) | Florida and southern Texas |

The effects NOAA lists grow with the level: weak power-grid fluctuations at G1, voltage alarms at high latitudes at G2, voltage corrections and satellite drag problems at G3, and possible widespread voltage-control problems and, at G5, grid collapse or transformer damage. Below Kp 5 there is no G level at all.

#### What are the R and S scales?

They rate two other things the Sun does, and neither depends on Kp.

**R: radio blackouts.** A solar flare's X-rays reach Earth in about eight minutes and ionise the sunlit upper atmosphere, which absorbs HF radio. The level is set by the flare's peak X-ray flux measured by the GOES satellites.

| R level | Flare class at peak | X-ray flux (W/m²) |
|---|---|---|
| R1 Minor | M1 | 10⁻⁵ |
| R2 Moderate | M5 | 5 × 10⁻⁵ |
| R3 Strong | X1 | 10⁻⁴ |
| R4 Severe | X10 | 10⁻³ |
| R5 Extreme | X20 | 2 × 10⁻³ |

Flare classes run A, B, C, M, X, each ten times stronger than the last, so an X1 flare is ten times an M1.

**S: solar radiation storms.** These rate energetic protons arriving at Earth, by the flux of protons of 10 MeV and above: S1 at 10 particle flux units, then 100, 1,000, 10,000 and 100,000 for S5. They matter to astronauts, polar flights and satellites.

A single eruption can trigger all three scales at different times: R within minutes of the flare, S within tens of minutes to hours, and G one to three days later when the ejected cloud of plasma arrives.

#### What is Hp30, and why use it next to Kp?

Kp's three-hour window hides fast changes. In 2022 GFZ introduced the Hpo family of indices, built the same way as Kp but with shorter windows: **Hp30** every 30 minutes and Hp60 every hour. Two differences matter:

- **Resolution.** A sharp substorm shows up in Hp30 within half an hour instead of being averaged into a three-hour block.
- **No ceiling.** Kp stops at 9. Hp30 is open-ended, so it can tell one extreme storm from a stronger one.

On a quiet day the two tell the same story. During a storm, Hp30 shows you its shape.

#### What do solar wind speed and Bz add?

Kp and the G scale describe what has already happened at the ground. The solar wind, measured by spacecraft about 1.5 million km upstream of Earth, shows what is about to happen.

- **Speed.** The slow wind is around 300 to 500 km/s. Streams from coronal holes and clouds from eruptions can exceed 600 to 800 km/s.
- **Bz.** The north–south component of the magnetic field carried by the wind. When Bz points south (negative), it links with Earth's field and energy pours in. A strongly negative Bz held for hours is the usual cause of a storm; a fast wind with northward Bz often does very little.

How to use these for one specific question is covered in [how to tell whether the aurora will be visible tonight](https://aisixteen.com/earth-around/blog/will-the-aurora-be-visible-tonight/).

#### Where does Earth Around fit?

[Earth Around](https://aisixteen.com/earth-around/) shows the current NOAA G, R and S levels in plain words, then the numbers behind them: Kp, Hp30 at 30-minute resolution, solar wind speed and Bz, and GOES X-ray flux. It runs on iPhone, iPad, Mac and Apple Watch. It needs a connection, because the data are live feeds from NOAA and GFZ. It has no account and no tracking. It displays measurements and the official scales; operational decisions for power grids, aviation or satellites belong with the official NOAA products.

#### Frequently asked questions

##### What Kp is a geomagnetic storm?

Kp 5 or higher. Kp 5 is G1 (minor), 6 is G2, 7 is G3, 8 is G4 and 9 is G5 (extreme).

##### Is Kp a forecast or a measurement?

A measurement of the past three hours. NOAA also issues Kp forecasts, which are predictions and are labelled as such.

##### Do solar flares cause geomagnetic storms?

Not directly. A flare's X-rays cause radio blackouts within minutes. Geomagnetic storms come from solar wind and from coronal mass ejections, which take one to three days to arrive.

#### Sources

- NOAA Space Weather Prediction Center, NOAA Space Weather Scales: [swpc.noaa.gov/noaa-scales-explanation](https://www.swpc.noaa.gov/noaa-scales-explanation)
- GFZ Helmholtz Centre for Geosciences, the Kp index and the Hpo indices (Hp30, Hp60): [kp.gfz.de](https://kp.gfz.de/en/)
- Yamazaki et al., "Geomagnetic Activity Index Hpo", *Geophysical Research Letters*, 2022: [doi.org/10.1029/2022GL098860](https://doi.org/10.1029/2022GL098860)

### How do tide predictions work, and can they be computed offline?

URL: https://aisixteen.com/marine-nav/blog/how-tide-predictions-work/ · App: Marine Nav (https://aisixteen.com/marine-nav/) · Published: 2026-11-24

Short answer: A tide prediction is the sum of a few dozen cosine waves, called harmonic constituents, each with a fixed astronomical period and a height and timing measured for one station. The constants are published, so the sum can be computed on a device with no connection. It predicts the astronomical tide only, not wind or surge.

A tide table looks like data from somewhere. It is really the output of a formula, and the same formula can run anywhere the station's constants are stored. That matters at sea, where a connection is the first thing to go.

![Marine Nav tide screen for San Francisco with the day's tide curve, high and low water times](https://aisixteen.com/marinenav/screenshot-960.webp "Marine Nav: a day's tide curve computed on the device from NOAA harmonic constants.")

#### What is the harmonic method?

The Moon and the Sun pull on the ocean with rhythms that astronomy gives exactly: the Moon passing overhead, the Sun passing overhead, the Moon's changing distance and tilt. Each rhythm produces a small regular rise and fall of the sea, a **constituent**, with a period that never changes.

What does change from port to port is how big each constituent is and how late it runs, because every bay and estuary responds differently. So for each station, a year or more of water-level measurements is analysed to find two numbers per constituent:

- its **amplitude** (how high), and
- its **phase lag** (how late, relative to the astronomical forcing).

Those are the **harmonic constants**. The predicted height at any moment is then:

**height = mean level + sum of [ f × amplitude × cos(speed × time + astronomical argument − phase lag) ]**

where *f* and the astronomical argument are slow corrections for the 18.6-year cycle of the Moon's orbit. NOAA's standard predictions use 37 constituents.

#### Which constituents matter most?

Usually five carry most of the tide.

| Constituent | Cause | Period (hours) |
|---|---|---|
| M2 | Principal lunar, twice daily | 12.42 |
| S2 | Principal solar, twice daily | 12.00 |
| N2 | The Moon's elliptical orbit | 12.66 |
| K1 | Lunar-solar, once daily | 23.93 |
| O1 | Lunar, once daily | 25.82 |

Three familiar facts fall out of this table:

- **Tides come about 50 minutes later each day**, because M2 repeats every 12 h 25 min, so two cycles take 24 h 50 min.
- **Springs and neaps.** M2 and S2 drift in and out of step every 14.77 days. In step, they add (spring tides, near new and full Moon). Out of step, they partly cancel (neap tides).
- **Mixed tides.** Where K1 and O1 are large compared with M2, as on the US west coast, the two high waters of a day have very different heights.

#### Why can this be computed offline?

Because nothing in the formula comes from a live measurement. The astronomy is known centuries ahead, and the station's constants are fixed numbers published by the hydrographic authority, in the US by NOAA's Center for Operational Oceanographic Products and Services. An app that stores the constants and does the sum gives the same predictions with the radio off as with it on.

Times need care. A tide table read in the wrong time zone is a navigational error, so a prediction should always state the zone it is in.

#### What do tide predictions leave out?

Everything that is not astronomy. The predicted height is the **astronomical tide**. The observed water level also includes:

- **Wind and pressure.** Onshore gales and low pressure raise the water; a deep low can add a storm surge of a metre or more. High pressure lowers it, roughly one centimetre per hectopascal.
- **River flow** in estuaries.
- **Seiches** and other local oscillations.

Heights are given above a **chart datum**. In the United States that is Mean Lower Low Water (MLLW), the average of the lower of each day's two low waters, so a predicted height can be negative on a low spring tide. Check which datum your chart uses before adding a tide height to a charted depth.

#### Is slack water at the same time as high water?

Often not. Tide (the vertical movement) and tidal current (the horizontal flow) are different predictions with their own constants. In many channels the current keeps flooding well after high water and turns an hour or more later. Use current predictions for slack water, never the tide table.

#### What is the rule of twelfths?

A mental approximation for a regular twice-daily tide: over the six hours between low and high water, the level changes by 1, 2, 3, 3, 2 and 1 twelfths of the range. With a 3.6 m range, the water rises 0.3 m in the first hour, 0.6 in the second, 0.9 in each of the middle two, then 0.6 and 0.3. It is a sine curve in round numbers, and it fails where the tide is mixed or distorted by shallow water. A computed curve is better whenever you have one.

#### Where does Marine Nav fit?

[Marine Nav](https://aisixteen.com/marine-nav/) carries NOAA's published harmonic constants for its stations and runs the harmonic synthesis on the device, so tide and tidal-current predictions, including slack water, work with no signal. Times are shown in the station's own time zone, labelled. Its predictions are validated against NOAA's own published predictions for the same stations. The limits are stated on screen: astronomical tide only, no storm surge or wind, and currents along the major axis only. The app also does magnetic declination from the World Magnetic Model 2025, great-circle distance and bearing, and celestial sight reduction. It is an aid to planning, not a substitute for official tide tables, charts or prudent seamanship.

#### Frequently asked questions

##### How accurate are tide predictions?

For the astronomical tide at a station with good constants, typically within a few centimetres and a few minutes. The observed level can differ much more when wind and pressure are unusual.

##### Why are there two high tides a day?

Because the Moon's pull raises water on the side of the Earth facing it and on the opposite side, and the Earth turns under both bulges. The main lunar constituent, M2, has a period of 12 hours 25 minutes.

##### Do tide predictions include storm surge?

No. They are the astronomical tide. Surge from wind and low pressure is forecast separately by the weather service.

#### Sources

- NOAA Center for Operational Oceanographic Products and Services, harmonic constituents and tide predictions: [tidesandcurrents.noaa.gov](https://tidesandcurrents.noaa.gov/about_harmonic_constituents.html)
- NOAA Special Publication NOS CO-OPS 3, *Tidal Analysis and Prediction* (2007): [tidesandcurrents.noaa.gov/publications](https://tidesandcurrents.noaa.gov/publications/Tidal_Analysis_and_Predictions.pdf)
- NOAA, tidal datums: [tidesandcurrents.noaa.gov/datum_options.html](https://tidesandcurrents.noaa.gov/datum_options.html)

### How is a loan payment calculated?

URL: https://aisixteen.com/par/blog/how-a-loan-payment-is-calculated/ · App: Par (https://aisixteen.com/par/) · Published: 2026-11-24

Short answer: A fixed loan payment is PMT = P × i ÷ (1 − (1 + i)^−n), where P is the amount borrowed, i is the interest rate per period and n is the number of payments. For 420,000 at 6.25% over 360 months, i is 0.0625 ÷ 12 and the payment is 2,586.01.

Every fixed-rate loan, from a car loan to a 30-year mortgage, is priced with one equation. Financial calculators call its five variables N, I/Y, PV, PMT and FV. This guide works the equation by hand so you can check any number a calculator or a lender gives you.

![Par time-value-of-money screen with a running tape of calculations beside it](https://aisixteen.com/par/screenshot-960.webp "Par: the calculation on the left, the tape of every solve on the right.")

#### What is the loan payment formula?

**PMT = P × i ÷ (1 − (1 + i)^−n)**

- **P** is the principal: the amount borrowed (PV on a calculator).
- **i** is the periodic rate: the annual note rate divided by the number of payments per year.
- **n** is the total number of payments (N).

The formula comes from one idea: the loan amount equals the present value of all the payments, each discounted at the loan's own rate.

#### How do you work it for a 30-year loan?

Take 420,000 borrowed at a 6.25% note rate, paid monthly for 30 years.

1. **Periodic rate:** 0.0625 ÷ 12 = 0.00520833.
2. **Number of payments:** 30 × 12 = 360.
3. **Growth factor:** (1.00520833)^360 = 6.4892.
4. **Denominator:** 1 − 1 ÷ 6.4892 = 0.84590.
5. **Numerator:** 420,000 × 0.00520833 = 2,187.50.
6. **Payment:** 2,187.50 ÷ 0.84590 = **2,586.01** per month.

Over 360 payments that is 930,964 in total, of which 510,964 is interest. The interest is larger than the loan, which is normal at this rate and term.

#### How does the payment split between interest and principal?

Each month, interest is charged on the balance still owed, and whatever is left of the payment reduces the balance.

| Payment | Interest | Principal | Balance after |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | 2,187.50 | 398.51 | 419,601.49 |
| 2 | 2,185.42 | 400.59 | 419,200.90 |
| 3 | 2,183.34 | 402.67 | 418,798.23 |

Interest for payment 2 is 419,601.49 × 0.00520833 = 2,185.42. The principal part grows a little every month, slowly at first: on this loan the balance does not fall below half until about year 21. That is why an extra payment early in a loan saves far more interest than the same payment late.

#### Why do calculators show the payment as a negative number?

Because of the cash-flow sign convention. Money you receive is positive, and money you pay out is negative. You receive the loan (PV = +420,000), so the payments are outflows (PMT = −2,586.01). If you enter both as positive, a calculator solving for the rate or the term will report an error, because no such loan can exist.

#### What is the difference between the note rate, APR and APY?

They answer three different questions, and regulations define two of them.

| Term | What it measures | Defined by |
|---|---|---|
| Note rate | The rate used to compute interest on the balance | The loan contract |
| APR | The yearly cost of credit including certain fees (the finance charge), expressed as a rate | Regulation Z (Truth in Lending), 12 CFR 1026 |
| APY | The yearly yield on a deposit including compounding | Regulation DD (Truth in Savings), 12 CFR 1030 |

**APR on a loan** is found by asking: given the payments, what rate makes them equal to the amount the borrower actually received after prepaid finance charges? In the example, if 6,000 of fees count as finance charges, the amount financed is 414,000 while the payment stays 2,586.01. Solving the same formula for the rate gives an APR of about 6.39%, above the 6.25% note rate.

**APY on a deposit** shows the effect of compounding: APY = (1 + r ÷ m)^m − 1. A 6.25% rate compounded monthly is (1.00520833)^12 − 1 = **6.43%**.

A loan's APR and a deposit's APY are not comparable; they are built differently on purpose.

#### Do the day-count rules change the answer?

For a standard monthly-payment loan, no: every month is treated as one twelfth of a year. Day count matters when interest accrues by the day, as on bonds, money-market instruments and some commercial loans.

- **30/360** treats every month as 30 days and the year as 360.
- **Actual/360** counts real days but divides by 360, which yields slightly more interest per year than the stated rate.
- **Actual/365** and **Actual/Actual** count real days over a 365-day or actual-length year.

On 1,000,000 at 6% for a 31-day month, 30/360 accrues 5,000.00, Actual/360 accrues 5,166.67 and Actual/365 accrues 5,095.89. Always check which convention a document names.

#### Where does Par fit?

[Par](https://aisixteen.com/par/) is an offline financial calculator with ten tools: time value of money, amortization, bonds, cash flow, day count, depreciation, percent, rate conversion, real estate and statistics. Each displayed result names the authority its method follows, such as CFPB Regulation Z and Regulation DD, the US Treasury, the IRS or NIST, and a running tape keeps every calculation so you can review it. It uses no network and has no account. It is a calculator, not financial advice, and it does not replace a lender's official disclosures.

#### Frequently asked questions

##### What is the monthly payment on 420,000 at 6.25% for 30 years?

2,586.01 for principal and interest. Taxes, insurance and any mortgage insurance are separate and are not part of the formula.

##### Why is APR higher than the interest rate?

Because APR spreads certain fees over the life of the loan. With no finance charges other than interest, APR and the note rate are the same.

##### How do I find the periodic rate?

Divide the annual note rate by the number of payments per year. For monthly payments at 6.25%, 0.0625 ÷ 12 = 0.00520833.

#### Sources

- Consumer Financial Protection Bureau, Regulation Z (Truth in Lending), 12 CFR Part 1026, including Appendix J on APR computation: [consumerfinance.gov](https://www.consumerfinance.gov/rules-policy/regulations/1026/)
- Consumer Financial Protection Bureau, Regulation DD (Truth in Savings), 12 CFR Part 1030, including Appendix A on APY: [consumerfinance.gov](https://www.consumerfinance.gov/rules-policy/regulations/1030/)

### How do you lay out studs 16 inches on center, and why does 19.2 exist?

URL: https://aisixteen.com/storypole/blog/stud-layout-16-on-center/ · App: Storypole (https://aisixteen.com/storypole/) · Published: 2026-11-24

Short answer: Hook the tape on the end of the plate, mark 15-1/4", then every 16" after that (31-1/4", 47-1/4"…), and set each stud just past its mark. That puts stud centres at 16", 32" and 48", so the edge of a 4-foot sheet lands on the middle of a stud. 19.2" is 96 ÷ 5: five bays per 8-foot sheet.

"On center" means the distance from the middle of one framing member to the middle of the next. The whole system exists so that 4 × 8 sheet goods always break on a stud. Once you see that, the odd numbers on a tape measure make sense.

![Storypole tape calculator showing 8 feet 10-1/4 inches on a draggable tape blade](https://aisixteen.com/storypole/screenshot-960.webp "Storypole: the answer lands on a tape you can drag.")

#### Why 16 inches, and why is the first mark at 15-1/4?

A sheet of plywood, OSB or drywall is 48" × 96". Both divide evenly by 16 and by 24, so a sheet edge always falls on the centre line of a stud, with half the stud's thickness left for the next sheet.

A stud is 1-1/2" thick, so its centre is 3/4" in from either face. For the centre of a stud to sit exactly 16" from the end of the wall, its near edge must be at 16 − 3/4 = **15-1/4"**.

The layout, measured from the outside end of the plate:

1. Mark **15-1/4"**. Draw a line and put an X on the far side of it. The stud covers the X.
2. Mark every 16" after that: **31-1/4", 47-1/4", 63-1/4", 79-1/4", 95-1/4"**.
3. Each stud's centre is now at 16", 32", 48", 64", 80" and 96".

Most tapes print the 16" multiples in red. Marking 3/4" back from each red number gives the same lines.

Lay out both plates together, clamped side by side, and always pull from the same end. Measuring stud to stud accumulates error; marks pulled from one end do not.

#### How many studs does a wall need?

Divide the wall length in inches by the spacing, round up, and add one for the starting end.

Example: a 14-foot wall (168") at 16" on center. 168 ÷ 16 = 10.5, round up to 11 spaces, so **12 studs**. The last regular stud is centred at 160", leaving a final bay of only 8" to the end stud. That short bay is normal. Do not stretch the spacing to even it out, or the sheets stop landing on studs.

That count is the plain wall only. Corners, intersecting walls, and the king, jack and cripple studs around each opening are extra, which is why estimators often carry one stud per foot of wall as a quick allowance.

#### What are the black diamonds on a tape measure?

They mark multiples of **19.2"**: 19-3/16", 38-3/8", 57-5/8", 76-13/16" and 96". The number is 96 ÷ 5, which gives five equal bays under an 8-foot sheet instead of six (16") or four (24").

| Spacing | Bays per 8 ft | Members per 8 ft run | Used for |
|---|---|---|---|
| 16" | 6 | 7 | Most walls and floors |
| 19.2" | 5 | 6 | Engineered I-joists and floor trusses |
| 24" | 4 | 5 | Roof trusses, advanced framing, some walls |

19.2" saves one member in every 8 feet compared with 16", while an 8-foot sheet laid across the framing still ends on a member. The catch is the 4-foot direction: 48 ÷ 19.2 = 2.5, so a sheet's 4-foot edge does not land on a member. That is why 19.2" is used where sheathing runs with its long side across the joists. The spacing is a consequence of sheet size, not a figure taken from a table.

#### How do you space balusters or slats evenly?

Equal spacing is a different problem: you choose the number of pieces, and the gap is whatever makes them fit.

**gap = (opening − number of pieces × piece width) ÷ (number of pieces + 1)**

The residential code adds a limit for guards: a 4" sphere must not pass through (IRC R312.1.3). So the gap has to be under 4".

Worked example: a 72" opening between posts, balusters 1-1/2" wide.

- With 12 balusters: (72 − 18) ÷ 13 = 4.15". Too wide.
- With 13 balusters: (72 − 19.5) ÷ 14 = **3.75"**, or 3-3/4". That passes.

For the marks, the first baluster's near edge is one gap from the post: 3-3/4". Each next one is a gap plus a width further on: 5-1/4" later. So the near edges fall at 3-3/4", 9", 14-1/4", 19-1/2" and so on, pulled from one end.

#### What size is a 2x4 really?

1-1/2" × 3-1/2". "2 × 4" is the nominal size; the dressed, dry size is smaller, and it is standardised in the American Softwood Lumber Standard, NIST PS 20.

| Nominal | Dressed (dry) |
|---|---|
| 2 × 4 | 1-1/2" × 3-1/2" |
| 2 × 6 | 1-1/2" × 5-1/2" |
| 2 × 8 | 1-1/2" × 7-1/4" |
| 2 × 10 | 1-1/2" × 9-1/4" |
| 2 × 12 | 1-1/2" × 11-1/4" |
| 1 × 4 | 3/4" × 3-1/2" |

Every layout number in this article depends on the 1-1/2" figure. With full-dimension or rough-sawn lumber, the 3/4" offset changes.

#### Where does Storypole fit?

[Storypole](https://aisixteen.com/storypole/) is a job-site calculator for carpenters, framers and remodelers. Its layout tools give on-center marks at 16", 19.2" and 24" with the odd last bay stated, and equal spacing as the full list of marks to pull rather than only a count. It also does feet-inch-fraction tape math in exact fractions, board feet and dressed lumber sizes, roof pitch and rafters, miters and bevels, concrete in cubic yards and wire gauge. It names the standard behind each sourced value and labels 19.2" as derived (96 ÷ 5) rather than sourced. It runs offline on iPhone, iPad, Mac and Apple Watch.

It does not measure: there is no camera and no AR ruler. It does the math on a measurement you already took with a tape.

#### Frequently asked questions

##### Where do you start measuring for 16 on center?

From the outside end of the plate. Make the first mark at 15-1/4" and every 16" after it, with each stud set on the far side of its mark.

##### What is 19.2 inches on a tape measure?

19-3/16", marked with a black diamond. It is 96" divided by 5, giving five bays per 8-foot sheet.

##### How far apart can deck or stair balusters be?

Close enough that a 4" sphere cannot pass between them under the International Residential Code, so the clear gap must be less than 4". Check your local code.

#### Sources

- NIST Voluntary Product Standard PS 20, *American Softwood Lumber Standard* (dressed sizes of lumber).
- International Residential Code 2021, section R312.1.3, Opening limitations: [codes.iccsafe.org](https://codes.iccsafe.org/content/IRC2021P2/chapter-3-building-planning)

### Why does altitude change HVAC air calculations?

URL: https://aisixteen.com/aircore/blog/altitude-correction-for-hvac-air-calculations/ · App: AirCore (https://aisixteen.com/aircore/) · Published: 2026-11-24

Short answer: The familiar air-side factors (1.08 for sensible heat, 0.68 or 4840 for latent, 4.5 for total) contain the density of standard sea-level air, 0.075 lb/ft³. Air is thinner at elevation, so each factor must be multiplied by the density ratio: about 0.83 at 5,000 ft, where 1.08 becomes 0.90.

Most air-side rules of thumb are the sea-level case of a more general equation. At a coastal site that does not matter. In Denver, Albuquerque or Mexico City it is a 17 to 25 percent error in airflow or capacity. This guide derives the factors, corrects them, and works one example.

![AirCore psychrometric screen with air-state inputs beside a psychrometric chart](https://aisixteen.com/aircore/screenshot-960.webp "AirCore: the air state as numbers and as a point on the chart.")

#### Where do 1.08, 4840 and 4.5 come from?

All three are a unit conversion wrapped around the density of standard air: 0.075 lb per cubic foot, which is dry air at about 70 °F and sea-level pressure (14.696 psia).

| Equation (IP units) | Factor | What is inside it |
|---|---|---|
| Sensible heat: q = 1.08 × cfm × ΔT | 1.08 | 0.075 lb/ft³ × 60 min/h × 0.24 Btu/lb·°F |
| Latent heat: q = 4840 × cfm × ΔW | 4840 | 0.075 × 60 × about 1,076 Btu/lb, with W in lb of water per lb of dry air |
| Latent heat, grains: q = 0.68 × cfm × Δgr | 0.68 | 4840 ÷ 7,000 grains per lb |
| Total heat: q = 4.5 × cfm × Δh | 4.5 | 0.075 × 60, with h in Btu/lb |

Check the first: 0.075 × 60 × 0.24 = 1.08. The 0.24 is the specific heat of dry air; some references use 1.10, which folds in a little moisture.

The point is that a fan moves **volume** (cfm), but heat is carried by **mass** (pounds of air). Density is the bridge between them, and density is what altitude changes.

#### How much thinner is the air at elevation?

The ASHRAE standard atmosphere gives barometric pressure from elevation Z in feet:

**p = 14.696 × (1 − 6.8754 × 10⁻⁶ × Z)^5.2559 psia**

At the same temperature, air density is proportional to pressure, so the density ratio is simply p ÷ 14.696.

| Elevation (ft) | Pressure (psia) | Density ratio | 1.08 becomes | 4.5 becomes |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 0 | 14.70 | 1.00 | 1.08 | 4.50 |
| 2,500 | 13.42 | 0.91 | 0.99 | 4.11 |
| 5,000 | 12.23 | 0.83 | 0.90 | 3.74 |
| 7,500 | 11.13 | 0.76 | 0.82 | 3.41 |
| 10,000 | 10.11 | 0.69 | 0.74 | 3.09 |

#### What does the correction do to a real number?

Take a supply fan delivering 2,000 cfm with a 20 °F temperature rise across a heating coil.

- **Sea-level factor:** q = 1.08 × 2,000 × 20 = **43,200 Btu/h**.
- **At 5,000 ft:** q = 1.08 × 0.832 × 2,000 × 20 = **35,900 Btu/h**.

The same fan, the same coil temperature rise, 17% less heat delivered. Turn it around: to deliver the full 43,200 Btu/h at 5,000 ft with a 20 °F rise, the fan must move 43,200 ÷ (0.899 × 20) = **about 2,400 cfm**.

This is why equipment selected from sea-level tables comes up short at altitude, and why a measured ΔT that "proves" capacity with the 1.08 factor overstates it.

#### Does altitude change the psychrometric chart too?

Yes. A printed psychrometric chart is drawn for one barometric pressure, usually sea level. At a lower pressure, air at the same dry-bulb temperature and relative humidity holds *more* water per pound of dry air, has a higher enthalpy and a larger specific volume.

Example, 75 °F and 50% relative humidity:

| Property | Sea level | 5,000 ft |
|---|---|---|
| Humidity ratio | about 65 gr/lb | about 78 gr/lb |
| Enthalpy | about 28.1 Btu/lb | about 30.2 Btu/lb |
| Specific volume | about 13.7 ft³/lb | about 16.5 ft³/lb |
| Dew point | about 55 °F | about 55 °F |

Dew point barely moves, because it depends on the vapour pressure, not on the total pressure. The other properties move enough to change a coil selection. ASHRAE publishes separate charts for 5,000 and 7,500 ft for this reason; software simply uses the right pressure.

#### How many properties do you need to fix an air state?

Two, plus the barometric pressure. Moist air has seven commonly used properties: dry bulb, wet bulb, dew point, relative humidity, humidity ratio, enthalpy and specific volume. Any two independent ones determine the rest. A few pairs do not work, because they carry the same information: dew point and humidity ratio, for example, are both statements of how much water is in the air.

#### Where does AirCore fit?

[AirCore](https://aisixteen.com/aircore/) is an air-side calculator for HVAC technicians, designers and contractors. You enter any two of the seven properties and it solves the rest and plots the point on a psychrometric chart. Site elevation sits in the toolbar of every screen, and every number is corrected to it, so the sea-level assumption cannot slip in unnoticed. It also does air-side heat in any direction, air mixing weighted by mass, duct sizing from friction, fan laws, and pipe sizing by Darcy–Weisbach or Hazen–Williams. Its psychrometric values are checked against CoolProp and IAPWS-95 reference data. It runs offline on iPhone, iPad, Mac and Apple Watch.

What it does not do: it has no fitting library and it does not perform load calculations. It computes air properties and sizes from the inputs you give it.

#### Frequently asked questions

##### What is the 1.08 factor at 5,000 ft?

About 0.90. Multiply 1.08 by the density ratio, 12.23 ÷ 14.696 = 0.832.

##### Do fans move less air at altitude?

A fan at a fixed speed moves the same volume (cfm) at any density, but less mass, so it carries less heat and develops less pressure. Fan power falls in the same proportion as density.

##### Does dew point change with altitude?

Very little for the same moisture content by vapour pressure. Humidity ratio, enthalpy and specific volume change noticeably.

#### Sources

- ASHRAE, *Handbook: Fundamentals*, chapter 1, Psychrometrics (standard atmosphere equation, moist-air properties, air-side heat equations).
- CoolProp, humid-air properties (HAPropsSI), an open reference implementation: [coolprop.org](http://www.coolprop.org/fluid_properties/HumidAir.html)
